rows.question: When does my maternity leave start if my due date is 15 November 2026?
rows.reply:
Under the Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) rules, the protected period before birth covers the last six weeks before the birth. The law says the employer may not employ a pregnant woman "in den letzten sechs Wochen vor der Entbindung" (in the last six weeks before the birth), unless she expressly declares she is willing to work. She can withdraw that declaration at any time for the future.

These six weeks are counted from the expected day of birth shown in a certificate from a doctor or midwife ("der voraussichtliche Tag der Entbindung ... wie er sich aus dem ärztlichen Zeugnis oder dem Zeugnis einer Hebamme ... ergibt"). So the count runs back six weeks from the date on that certificate, which in your question is 15 November 2026. The excerpts do not set out how the first day of the six weeks is counted, so this answer does not fix an exact start date.

If the baby is born earlier or later than the expected day, the period before the birth becomes shorter or longer to match. After the birth, the protected period lasts eight weeks. It is extended to twelve weeks for premature births, multiple births, and, on application, where a disability of the child is medically confirmed within eight weeks. If the birth is early, the period after the birth is also extended by the time lost before it.

The Mutterschutz Act does not cover self-employed people.

During the protected periods, statutory health insurance members can receive Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity benefit) from their health insurance fund (Krankenkasse). For payment before the birth, the doctor's or midwife's certificate giving the expected day of birth is what counts.

Whether and how these rules apply to you is not decided here. Your employer applies the protected period, and your Krankenkasse decides on maternity benefit.

rows.question: How long after birth can we apply for Elterngeld without losing money?
rows.reply:
The law does not set an application deadline. It limits how far back payment goes. Elterngeld (parental allowance) is paid retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the month in which your application is received. The statute says it is "rückwirkend nur für die letzten drei Lebensmonate vor Beginn des Lebensmonats geleistet, in dem der Antrag auf Elterngeld eingegangen ist". Months of the child's life count from the birth date, not calendar months.

Elterngeld can be drawn from the day of birth ("Es kann ab dem Tag der Geburt bezogen werden"). So any month of the child's life that falls more than three months before the month your application arrives is not paid. Applications more than three months after the birth lose whole months of payment.

The application must be made in writing ("Elterngeld ist schriftlich zu beantragen"). Your Elterngeldstelle handles the application and decides on it.

rows.question: How much notice do I have to give my employer for Elternzeit?
rows.reply:
Elternzeit (parental leave (unpaid job-protected leave)) is not applied for. You request it from your employer in text form. The notice period depends on when the leave falls.

- Leave before your child's third birthday: at least seven weeks before the leave begins ("spätestens sieben Wochen ... vor Beginn der Elternzeit").
- Leave between the third birthday and the end of the child's eighth year: at least 13 weeks before the leave begins ("spätestens 13 Wochen").

When you request leave for the period before the third birthday, you must also state at the same time which periods within two years you will take as Elternzeit. For urgent reasons, a reasonable shorter period is possible by exception ("Bei dringenden Gründen ist ausnahmsweise eine angemessene kürzere Frist möglich"). If a mother cannot request leave directly after her maternity protection period in time, for a reason that is not her fault, she can make the request within one week after that reason ends. The employer must confirm the Elternzeit to you.

Text form means the notice can be, for example, an unsigned letter or an email.

The Familienportal page describes a different rule for children born before 1 July 2015, with seven weeks for all periods. The statute excerpts here do not contain that transitional rule, so I cannot confirm it from the law. Whether a shorter period is acceptable in your case depends on the circumstances, and these excerpts do not say who decides that.

rows.question: How long is maternity protection after the birth if the baby comes early?
rows.reply:
After the birth, Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) normally lasts eight weeks. During this time the employer may not employ the mother ("bis zum Ablauf von acht Wochen nach der Entbindung nicht beschäftigen").

When the baby comes early, the law adds time in two ways:

1. If the birth counts as a premature birth ("bei Frühgeburten"), the period after the birth is extended from eight to twelve weeks. The same twelve weeks apply to multiple births.

2. If the baby arrives before the expected date, the period before the birth is shorter than six weeks. The days lost before the birth are added to the period after it ("verlängert sich die Schutzfrist nach der Entbindung ... um den Zeitraum der Verkürzung der Schutzfrist vor der Entbindung"). This applies to the eight-week period and to the twelve-week period.

The statute does not define when a birth counts as premature. The federal family portal gives one example: a birth weight under 2,500 grams. It describes the result as a total period of 18 weeks instead of 14.

The excerpts do not say who confirms that a birth counts as premature, or how the extension is recorded.

rows.question: Can my employer dismiss me while I am pregnant?
rows.reply:
In general, no. During pregnancy your employer is not allowed to dismiss you. There are narrow exceptions, and they need an authority's approval.

The Kündigungsschutz (protection against dismissal) in the Maternity Protection Act says dismissal is not permitted ("Die Kündigung gegenüber einer Frau ist unzulässig"):
- during pregnancy;
- until four months after a miscarriage after the twelfth week of pregnancy;
- until the end of the protection period after the birth, and at least until four months after the birth.

This protection applies if your employer knows about the pregnancy when giving notice. It also applies if you tell them "innerhalb von zwei Wochen nach Zugang der Kündigung" (within two weeks of receiving the notice). Missing those two weeks does no harm if the delay was not your fault and you give the information without delay. The guidance page adds that you are protected even if you did not yet know you were pregnant, but you must already have been pregnant when the notice reached you.

The exception: the highest state authority responsible for occupational safety, or a body it designates, can declare a dismissal permissible "ausnahmsweise" (exceptionally). This applies only in special cases unrelated to your condition. The dismissal must then be in writing and must state the reason. The guidance page gives examples such as insolvency, the partial closure of the business, or a particularly serious breach of duty. It says that without the authority's approval the dismissal is "unwirksam" (ineffective).

If you are dismissed without that approval, the guidance page says you must bring a claim before the labour court. It says this must "normalerweise innerhalb von 3 Wochen" (normally within 3 weeks) be filed, counted from receipt of the written notice. If you do not bring a claim, the dismissal counts as legally effective. The page also says you should involve the responsible supervisory authority.

Whether a particular dismissal is permissible is decided by the state supervisory authority and, if challenged, by the labour court. The excerpts do not name the specific office in Hessen.

rows.question: Is there an income limit above which we get no Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Under federal law, the right to Elterngeld (parental allowance) lapses above a set level of zu versteuerndes Einkommen (taxable income).

What the statute says (BEEG §1 Abs. 8):
- For one entitled person, the claim lapses if their zu versteuerndes Einkommen in the last completed tax assessment period before the birth was more than 175,000 euros ("in Höhe von mehr als 175 000 Euro").
- If another person also meets the entitlement conditions, the claim lapses if the combined zu versteuerndes Einkommen of both is more than 175,000 euros ("wenn die Summe des zu versteuernden Einkommens beider Personen mehr als 175 000 Euro beträgt").

Taxable income is not gross income. The official Familienportal explains that gross income is usually much higher, because items such as special expenses, provision expenses, allowances and extraordinary burdens are deducted first. The Finanzamt determines your zu versteuerndes Einkommen, and it appears in your tax assessment (Steuerbescheid).

If the tax assessment for that year is not yet available when you apply, the statute provides for payment subject to revocation or a provisional decision (BEEG §8 Abs. 2 and 3).

The Familienportal also describes different, higher limits for births before 1 April 2025. The transitional provision that governs earlier births is not among the excerpts I was given, so I cannot say which limit applies to which birth. That is decided by the responsible Elterngeldstelle.

Whether your family is above or below the limit is not something I can assess. Only the Elterngeldstelle decides an individual application.

rows.question: How many months of Elterngeld can we get in total?
rows.reply:
The total depends on which type of Elterngeld (parental allowance) you choose and how you share it. These are the general rules in the law. They are not an assessment of your family.

Basic Elterngeld: parents together are entitled to 12 monthly amounts ("zwölf Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld"). There are 2 further months ("Partnermonate") if one parent's earned income is reduced in two months of the child's life. One parent can receive at most 12 monthly amounts of basic Elterngeld. Each parent must receive Elterngeld for at least two months ("mindestens für zwei Lebensmonate") to be entitled to it at all.

Elterngeld Plus: instead of one month of basic Elterngeld, a parent can take two months of Elterngeld Plus ("jeweils zwei Lebensmonate Elterngeld Plus").

Partnership bonus: on top of the 12 months, each parent can receive up to four monthly amounts of partnership bonus ("höchstens vier zustehenden Monatsbeträge Partnerschaftsbonus"). The federal Familienportal explains that this applies when both parents work part-time at the same time.

Time limits within the child's life: basic Elterngeld can be received until the child completes the 14th month of life. Elterngeld Plus can be received until the child completes the 32nd month of life, as long as at least one parent takes it in consecutive months from the 15th month onward.

Premature births: if the child was born at least 6, 8, 12 or 16 weeks before the expected delivery date, the parents' joint entitlement rises to 13, 14, 15 or 16 monthly amounts of basic Elterngeld. The period to receive it is extended to match. The expected date on the doctor's or midwife's certificate is what counts.

Months are counted as months of the child's life, not calendar months. Only the Elterngeld office that handles your application decides how many months your family receives.

rows.question: What is the Partnerschaftsbonus and who qualifies?
rows.reply:
The Partnerschaftsbonus (partnership bonus months) gives each parent extra months of the part-time variant of parental allowance, paid when both parents work part-time at the same time.

What the law says (BEEG §4b):
- Both parents must work "nicht weniger als 24 und nicht mehr als 32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats". This means at least 24 and at most 32 hours a week, averaged over the month of the child's life.
- Both parents must also meet the general conditions for parental allowance in BEEG §1. The excerpts provided do not set out those conditions.
- If both conditions are met, each parent is entitled to one additional monthly amount for that month.
- Each parent can receive at most four bonus months. The bonus can only be drawn for at least two months.
- Both parents must draw it at the same time, in consecutive months of the child's life.
- Suppose it turns out during or after the bonus period that the conditions were not met in every month applied for. The requirement for consecutive months still counts as met.

The Familienportal adds two practical points. If either parent works fewer than 24 or more than 32 hours on average in a month, the bonus for that month must be repaid by both parents. The other months are not affected if the conditions were met in at least 2 of them. The same page says the bonus is calculated in the same way as the part-time variant and is between 150 and 900 euros a month per parent, depending on income before the birth.

Single parents (BEEG §4c): one parent can draw the bonus alone in certain cases:
- the parent meets the conditions for the tax relief for single parents and the other parent lives with neither them nor the child;
- care by the other parent would endanger the child's welfare; or
- care by the other parent is impossible, for example because of serious illness or severe disability.

That parent must work 24 to 32 hours a week on average in two to four consecutive months.

The Familienportal notes that its explanations apply to children born after August 2021. For children born before 1 September 2021, partly different rules apply.

Whether a particular family qualifies, and for how much, is decided by the Elterngeldstelle.

rows.question: How quickly do we have to register the birth at the Standesamt?
rows.reply:
The birth must be reported to the Standesamt (civil registry office) for the place where the child was born within one week. The law says the birth is to be reported "binnen einer Woche" (within one week) to the Standesamt "in dessen Zuständigkeitsbereich es geboren ist" (in whose area the child was born). Under the law, the report can come from certain persons, orally or in writing, or from certain institutions, in writing.

Who does it depends on where the child was born:
- Hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic: the facility notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends the birth confirmation. You give the facility the first name and surname you have chosen, and it passes them on.
- Home birth: the midwife or doctor issues the birth confirmation, and you must present it to the responsible Standesamt within one week. You tell the Standesamt the chosen names directly.

One official checklist says "innerhalb von 7 Werktagen" (within 7 working days). The statute says "binnen einer Woche" (within one week), and that is the rule given here.

If you have not decided on a name, you must tell the responsible Standesamt within one month. After that, the Standesamt must inform the family court, which then chooses one parent to decide the name.

The Standesamt in the place of birth lists on its website which other documents you need.

rows.question: Does my Krankenkasse pay for a midwife?
rows.reply:
Under federal law, a woman with statutory health insurance is entitled to midwife help as a benefit of that insurance. Your Krankenkasse (statutory health insurer) is the body that provides it.

What the law covers (SGB V §24d):
- Medical care and midwife help during pregnancy, at the birth, and after the birth.
- This includes the examinations to confirm the pregnancy and prenatal check-ups.
- Midwife help for care after the birth (the postnatal period) runs "bis zum Ablauf von zwölf Wochen nach der Geburt" (until twelve weeks after the birth). Anything beyond that needs a doctor's order ("bedürfen der ärztlichen Anordnung").
- If the mother cannot care for the child after the birth, the insured child is entitled to the midwife help that relates to the child.

The federal family portal puts it simply: every woman with statutory health insurance is entitled to support from a Hebamme (midwife). If you have private health insurance, the portal says to check with your insurer beforehand which services it covers.

Whether these rules apply to you, and what is covered in your case, is decided by your Krankenkasse. If you are privately insured, your private insurer decides.

rows.question: How do we insure the baby after the birth?
rows.reply:
Under federal law, the statutory health insurance covers the children of its members through Familienversicherung (free family cover for dependants). SGB V §10(1) says the children of members are insured ("Versichert sind ... die Kinder von Mitgliedern") if they meet these conditions:

- They live or normally stay in Germany ("ihren Wohnsitz oder gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland haben").
- They are not insured in their own right and are not voluntarily insured.
- They are not exempt from compulsory insurance.
- They are not self-employed as their main occupation.
- Their own income does not regularly exceed one seventh of the monthly reference amount.

Under §10(2), children are covered up to age 18. Cover can continue longer in certain situations, such as education or disability.

There is one important exception in §10(3). A child is not insured through the member if three things are all true:

- The other parent (the member's spouse or partner, related to the child) is not a member of a Krankenkasse.
- That parent's total income regularly exceeds one twelfth of the annual earnings ceiling ("ein Zwölftel der Jahresarbeitsentgeltgrenze").
- That income is regularly higher than the member's.

To register the baby with the Krankenkasse, you need the birth certificate. The Standesamt (registry office) issues it. The birth must be registered there within 1 week, at the office responsible for the place of birth. If the baby is born in a hospital or birth centre, the facility notifies the Standesamt.

The excerpts do not describe the rest of the registration procedure, and they do not cover private health insurance. Whether Familienversicherung applies to your child is decided by your Krankenkasse (statutory health insurer). Ask it what it needs from you.

rows.question: When are the first check-ups for the baby?
rows.reply:
The first check-ups are set out in the Kinder-Richtlinie (children's early-detection guideline) of the Gemeinsamer Bundesausschuss. It provides ten check-ups in the first six years, named U1 to U9 (including U7a).

The first ones are:

- U1: directly after birth ("Unmittelbar nach der Geburt"). It should take place within the first 30 minutes after the baby is born ("innerhalb der ersten 30 Minuten nach der Geburt"). If no doctor is present but a midwife is, the midwife should do it.
- U2: 3rd to 10th day of life ("3.-10. Lebenstag"). The tolerance limit is the 3rd to 14th day ("3.-14. Lebenstag").
- U3: 4th to 5th week of life ("4.-5. Lebenswoche"). The tolerance limit is the 3rd to 8th week ("3.-8. Lebenswoche").
- U4: 3rd to 4th month of life ("3.-4. Lebensmonat"). The tolerance limit is the 2nd to 4½ month ("2.-4 ½ Lebensmonat").

The guideline says the check-ups can only be used within these periods, taking the tolerance limits into account ("können nur in den jeweils angegebenen Zeiträumen unter Berücksichtigung folgender Toleranzgrenzen in Anspruch genommen werden").

For babies born early, the same periods still apply ("Auch bei Frühgeborenen sind die Untersuchungszeiträume einzuhalten"). Being born early is taken into account when the results are assessed.

The G-BA page notes that the published version does not yet include a decision that came into force on 20 August 2026. Check the current version with the G-BA or your child's doctor.

rows.question: What is Mutterschaftsgeld and when do I apply for it?
rows.reply:
Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is a payment for the protection periods before and after the birth, and for the day of the birth itself.

Who pays it depends on how you are insured:

- If you are a member of a statutory health insurer, you receive Mutterschaftsgeld under the rules of the Social Code, Book V (MuSchG §19(1)). For members who are employed when the protection period before the birth starts, it equals average net daily pay over the last three settled calendar months, but it is "höchstens 13 Euro für den Kalendertag" (at most 13 euros per calendar day) (SGB V §24i(2)).
- If your average pay is higher than 13 euros a day, your employer pays the difference as a separate top-up, the "Zuschuss zum Mutterschaftsgeld" (MuSchG §20(1)).
- If you are not a member of a statutory health insurer, you receive Mutterschaftsgeld paid by the federal government, but "insgesamt höchstens 210 Euro" (at most 210 euros in total). It is paid "auf Antrag vom Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung" (on application, by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung) (MuSchG §19(2)).

The protection periods normally begin 6 weeks before the expected birth date and end 8 weeks after the birth ("beginnen normalerweise 6 Wochen vor dem errechneten Geburtstermin und enden 8 Wochen nach der Geburt"). For payment before the birth, the law relies on a certificate from a doctor or midwife stating the expected date of delivery ("das Zeugnis eines Arztes oder einer Hebamme") (SGB V §24i(3)).

While you receive pay from your employer that is subject to contributions, the claim to Mutterschaftsgeld is suspended for that time (SGB V §24i(4)). Mutterschaftsgeld from a statutory health insurer and the employer top-up for the time from the birth onwards are counted against Elterngeld. The 210-euro payment from the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung is not (BEEG §3(1)).

When to apply: the excerpts do not say when or how to apply. If you are in statutory health insurance, ask your health insurer. If you are not, ask the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung, which pays on application. Whether you qualify, and how much you would receive, is decided by that body, or by your employer for the top-up.

rows.question: We are not married. Is my partner automatically the legal father?
rows.reply:
No. Under German law, a man is the legal father in one of three ways: he is married to the mother at the time of the birth, he has acknowledged paternity, or a court has established his paternity (BGB §1592). Being the partner is not one of them.

If you are not married when the child is born, your partner has to make a Vaterschaftsanerkennung (acknowledgement of paternity) to count as the legal father. It is voluntary and needs the mother's consent. It can be made before the birth (BGB §1594 (4)).

It has no effect while another man's paternity exists (BGB §1594 (2)). For example, if the mother is married to another man at the time of the birth, that husband is the legal father.

The father makes his declaration in person at a responsible office, such as the youth welfare office, a registry office, a local court or a notary. The mother also has to give her consent in person. The office records both. Depending on the state, a notary or local court may charge a fee.

If there is no Vaterschaftsanerkennung, the child, the mother or the presumed biological father can ask a court to establish paternity.

Being the legal father does not on its own give him parental custody. For that, both parents must declare that they want joint custody, or a family court must decide. Marrying after the birth also gives joint custody.

The official family portal notes that some of its information on this topic is being updated after a recent change in the law. Your local youth welfare office advises on paternity and custody.

rows.question: How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
rows.reply:
If the parents are not married to each other when the child is born, the mother has parental custody on her own. Under federal law, unmarried parents get joint custody in one of three ways.

1. Both parents make declarations that they want to take on custody jointly, called a Sorgeerklärung (declaration of joint custody). These can be made at the youth welfare office or before a notary, for example. They can also be made before the child is born.

2. The parents marry each other after the birth.

3. The family court transfers joint custody to both parents on the application of one parent. The court does this if joint custody does not go against the child's welfare. If the other parent gives no reasons against it, within a period the court sets, and none are otherwise apparent, the law presumes that joint custody does not go against the child's welfare. In that case the court decides in a simplified procedure, without hearing the youth welfare office and without hearing the parents in person.

Before any of this, the father must first be legally recognised as the father. This happens if he acknowledges the child as his own with the mother's consent, or if a court establishes paternity. Recognising paternity does not by itself give him custody. A Sorgeerklärung or a court decision is still needed.

Your local youth welfare office advises on all questions about parental custody. Where joint custody is contested, the family court decides.

rows.question: We are getting Mutterschaftsgeld. Does that reduce our Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, as a general rule. The law says Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is offset against Elterngeld (parental allowance). This applies to Mutterschaftsgeld from a statutory health insurer and to the employer's top-up to it. It covers only payments due 'für die Zeit ab dem Tag der Geburt des Kindes' (for the time from the day of the child's birth). Payments for the weeks before the birth are not offset.

One exception: the one-off Mutterschaftsgeld of at most 210 euros, paid by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung to women who are not members of a statutory health insurer, is not offset.

What the offset means, according to the official family portal:
- Maternity benefits for the same child are offset in full ('komplett auf das Elterngeld angerechnet').
- If the maternity benefits are higher than the Elterngeld, only the maternity benefits are paid.
- If the Elterngeld is higher, the difference is paid as Elterngeld on top.
- The offset is calculated by the day. If maternity benefits end partway through a month of the child's life, Elterngeld is paid for the remaining days of that month.
- For the mother, any month in which she is entitled to maternity benefits for the same child counts as a month of basic Elterngeld ('Basiselterngeld'). Being entitled for a single day in that month is enough.
- The maternity benefits are offset only against the mother's Elterngeld, not against the father's.

This is the general rule. How it applies to your family, and any amount, is decided by the office that handles your Elterngeld application.

rows.question: Can I work while receiving Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, working is not ruled out. The law lists, as one condition for Elterngeld (parental allowance), that the person "keine oder keine volle Erwerbstätigkeit ausübt", meaning they do no paid work or do not work full-time (BEEG §1(1) no. 4).

The federal family portal says you may work part-time while receiving Elterngeld if you work no more than 32 hours a week. The portal says this explanation covers children born after August 2021. If your child was born before 1 September 2021, partly different rules apply, and the portal refers you to your Elterngeldstelle.

Working affects the amount. For months after the birth in which you earn less than you did before the birth, Elterngeld is paid as a percentage of the difference between the two incomes. For this calculation, pre-birth income counts up to a maximum of 2,770 euros (BEEG §2(3)).

What your application states also matters:
- If the application says you expect income from work during the payment period, the amount is decided provisionally at first (BEEG §8(3) no. 3). After the payment period ends, you must prove the income you actually earned (BEEG §8(1)).
- If the application says you expect no income from work, Elterngeld is paid on the condition that it can be revoked if you do earn income (BEEG §8(2)).

How these rules apply to you, including your hours and amount, is decided by your Elterngeldstelle.

rows.question: Where and how do we apply for Kindergeld?
rows.reply:
Where: Kindergeld (child benefit) is applied for at the Familienkasse responsible for you. The law says this is the Familienkasse in whose district you have your residence ("in deren Bezirk der Berechtigte seinen Wohnsitz hat"). The official family portal says to submit the application to the Familienkasse of your Agentur für Arbeit, which is "in der Regel" (as a rule) the one that handles it. If you have questions about applying, the portal gives the free Bundesagentur für Arbeit service number: 0800 4 555530.

How: The law says Kindergeld must be applied for in writing ("schriftlich zu beantragen"). The family portal says you can apply electronically or in writing, using the Familienkassen form. You can fill it in online, then print and sign it. For newborn children, you can also apply fully online with a valid ELSTER certificate, with no printing or handwritten signature.

What to include: The application must give your tax identification number and your child's tax identification number. If your child was born abroad or lives abroad, the Bundesagentur für Arbeit asks for a copy of the foreign birth certificate, or another official document certifying the birth. If the Familienkasse needs more documents, it will tell you the date by which to send them. Missing that date can delay your application or lead to it being refused.

Who applies: Kindergeld for a child is paid to only one person. If the child lives in the shared household of both parents, the parents decide between themselves who is the entitled person. Besides the entitled person, anyone with a legitimate interest in the payment may also file the application.

Backdating: The family portal says Kindergeld can be paid retroactively for up to 6 months. If you are applying for earlier months, state in the application that you are applying retroactively and from when you want to receive Kindergeld.

Whether you are entitled, and from when, is decided by the Familienkasse.

rows.question: What are the Elterngeld rules for a self-employed parent in Bavaria?
rows.reply:
Bavaria's state procedures are outside what this product covers. We cover federal law, Hessen's procedures and the Indian consular track. For how to apply in Bavaria, contact the Elterngeld office responsible for where you live there.

The federal rules below apply everywhere in Germany, including Bavaria. Only the responsible Elterngeld office decides whether you qualify and how much you would get.

Who can claim. Elterngeld (parental allowance) can be claimed by someone who lives in Germany, lives with the child in one household, cares for and brings up the child themselves, and works not at all or not full-time (BEEG §1(1)).

How self-employed income counts. Elterngeld is 67 percent of income from work before the birth. That income includes positive income from a trade or business and from self-employed work under §2(1) sentence 1 nos. 1 to 3 of the Income Tax Act, if it is taxable in Germany. Taxes and social contributions are deducted (BEEG §2(1)). For months with no income from work, the monthly maximum is 1,800 euros (BEEG §2(1)), and the minimum is 300 euros (BEEG §2(4)). The 67 percent rises for pre-birth income under 1,000 euros, up to 100 percent. It falls for pre-birth income over 1,200 euros, down to 65 percent (BEEG §2(2)).

If you keep working after the birth. For months with lower income than before the birth, Elterngeld is paid as that percentage of the difference. At most 2,770 euros counts as pre-birth income (BEEG §2(3)).

Provisional decisions. The amount is first decided provisionally, based on the information you have made credible, in three cases: when the tax assessment for the last completed assessment period before the birth is not yet available and it cannot yet be said whether the limits in §1(8) are exceeded; when pre-birth income cannot be determined; or when you expect income from work during the payment period (BEEG §8(3)). If you stated expected income in the application, you must prove your actual income for that time once the payment period ends (BEEG §8(1)). If you stated you would have no income, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation in case you do have income (BEEG §8(2)).

How long. The basic form can be drawn until the child completes its 14th month of life. The Plus form can be drawn until the 32nd month, under the conditions in the law. A parent must draw Elterngeld for at least two months of the child's life (BEEG §4(1), §4(4)).

The responsible Elterngeld office in Bavaria decides your individual case.

rows.question: Can you fill in our Elterngeld application form for us?

We cannot fill in your application. Completing the form means making choices and statements about your family, such as which months to claim, and that is an individual case decision only you and the responsible authority can make. Here is what the law says the application involves.

The responsible authority is the one your Land has designated for the district where your child lives at the time of the first application. That office decides your application and can tell you which form to use.

rows.question: How much tax will we save if I switch to Steuerklasse 3 before the birth?
rows.reply:
We cannot tell you how much tax you would save by switching tax class. Calculating tax owed or saved, and advising on which tax class to choose, is individual tax advice that only a tax adviser or your tax office can give.

What the excerpts do cover is how a tax class change before the birth is treated when parental allowance is calculated:

- When parental allowance is calculated, the income tax deduction takes your tax class into account, and the factor if you have one. Tax class VI is disregarded.
- A tax class change before the birth can affect the amount of your taxes and social contributions.
- For the simplified net-income calculation, the newest tax class is used. The older tax class is used only if it applied for longer than the newer one within the whole assessment period. The same rule applies to other deduction details, such as the number of child allowances.
- If you work after the birth, the same deduction details as before the birth are used. Changing tax class again after the birth has no further effect on your parental allowance.

The parental allowance office calculates the net income figure itself, using a simplified method. It decides what amount applies to you. For the tax effect of switching class, ask a tax adviser or your tax office.
